ideas.title: Open-Weight Models Are the New Linux
ideas.summary: The trajectory of open-weight AI mirrors the rise of Linux: infrastructure gets commoditized, value moves up the stack.
ideas.angle: Analyze historical parallels between open-source OS adoption and open-weight model licensing; what startups should build on top that isn't just a model wrapper.

ideas.title: When to Build an Agent Instead of a Workflow
ideas.summary: Autonomous agents are trendy, but deterministic workflows are often more reliable. The real skill is knowing when autonomy genuinely solves a user problem.
ideas.angle: A decision framework based on task variability, error tolerance, and user trust; case studies of agent vs. workflow in real products.

ideas.title: Code Review as a UX Problem
ideas.summary: Most code review tools are designed for tracking, not for human understanding. Great developer UX can make reviews faster and more meaningful.
ideas.angle: Evaluate code review tools through the lens of cognitive load, inline context, and async communication; what a well-designed review experience looks like.

ideas.title: Refactoring as a Product Skill
ideas.summary: Refactoring is often framed as engineering debt, but it's actually a strategic way to keep product velocity high as scope expands.
ideas.angle: Shift the conversation from code quality to feature delivery: how disciplined refactoring lets small teams outpace competitors who add features without cleanup.

ideas.title: Local-First Software Is a Protocol, Not a Feature
ideas.summary: The local-first movement isn't just about offline mode—it's about rethinking where data lives and how synchronization happens.
ideas.angle: Explore the protocol layer (CRDTs, sync engines) as the real innovation; why apps that treat local-first as a tradeoff miss the point.

ideas.title: The Developer Tools Boring Barometer
ideas.summary: The best developer tools are often 'boring'—they do one thing reliably and don't change often. Excitement is a warning sign.
ideas.angle: A contrarian metric for evaluating dev tools: measure how little you notice them, not how many features they have; examples from git, SSH, and cron.

ideas.title: Pricing AI Features by Job-to-Be-Done
ideas.summary: AI features have unpredictable marginal costs, which makes pricing tricky. The right model depends more on perceived value than on cost accounting.
ideas.angle: Map AI feature types to pricing models: when per-use aligns with bursts of value, when seats fit habitual use, and when bundling removes adoption friction.

ideas.title: One-File Tools as a Design Philosophy
ideas.summary: A single-file tool forces constraints: fewer abstractions, easier auditing, and a clear mental model. That's a feature, not a hack.
ideas.angle: Look at one-file software as a reaction to framework bloat; what constraints teach about essential complexity and usability.
